identification.summary: Storm-2945 is a Microsoft designation for an actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses is an operational sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, based on technical and operational overlaps [S1]. It is tied to the CaptiveCrunch campaign, which manipulates traffic on hospitality and guest Wi-Fi networks served by captive portals to reach corporate travelers' accounts and devices [S1]. Microsoft observed the actor using AI to support a significant portion of its operations [S1].
identification.firstObserved: February 2026: AI-augmented device code and OAuth phishing leading to Entra device registration and Microsoft 365 data collection [S1]. Captive-portal traffic manipulation observed from early May 2026 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft's July 2026 post names the campaign CaptiveCrunch; Microsoft updated it on 2026-10-05 [S1]. Microsoft says the campaign is distinct from the Forest Blizzard DNS hijacking operation it disclosed in April 2026, though some TTPs are similar [S1]. Some secondary press (citing ReliaQuest tradecraft comparisons) ties related activity to APT28; Microsoft's own post ties Storm-2945 to Midnight Blizzard, so the two should not be merged [S1]. Storm-2945 is not the same as Storm-2949, a separate Microsoft-tracked cloud identity actor [S3].

attribution.sponsor: Russia (via Midnight Blizzard). Microsoft describes Midnight Blizzard as Russia-based and notes that US and UK governments have attributed it to the SVR [S1]. Microsoft does not independently name a state sponsor for Storm-2945 beyond its sub-cluster assessment [S1].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft assesses Storm-2945 is an operational sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard [S1]. Microsoft also cautions that some 'Suspicious activity linked to a Russian state-sponsored threat actor' Defender alerts may stem from unrelated actors [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft cites technical and operational overlaps: similarities to Storm-2372 (device code and OAuth phishing), Microsoft Graph email exfiltration, social engineering over commercial messaging apps, and similar victimology [S1].

objectives: Access the accounts and devices of corporate travelers and, through stolen tokens, their enterprise cloud environments [S1]. Microsoft's reporting describes the activity as espionage-style credential, session and data theft; it does not state a specific intelligence requirement [S1].

sectors: Hospitality (hotels, conference centers and other shared venues with captive portals, as access points) [S1]
Corporate travelers using guest Wi-Fi (end victims) [S1]
regions: Wi-Fi networks at hospitality-related organizations in 'several countries'; Microsoft does not name them [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft reports Windows targeting and indications of Android targeting via APK installs in ClickFix landing pages [S1]. Common equipment and management systems across affected networks suggest access to shared services in the captive portal ecosystem rather than isolated venue compromises [S1]. Microsoft cites Black Lotus Labs reporting for the possibility of continued access to upstream hospitality managed service providers [S1]. Specific countries and victim industries reported only in secondary summaries are listed under gaps.

capabilities.summary: Compromise of captive portal or Wi-Fi equipment (initial vector still under investigation), then redirection of DNS and HTTP traffic through actor infrastructure when browsers run connectivity checks [S1]. Lures include fake browser or OS updates and ClickFix-style verification prompts [S1]. Payloads are CornFlake, a Go RAT with configurable fake-update windows, redundant persistence (service, Run keys, scheduled tasks, watchdog), AMSI tampering, sandbox timing checks and silent UAC bypasses, plus an October 2026 Rust variant consistent with AI-enabled development [S1]. ChocoShell is an in-memory PowerShell infostealer for browser cookies, passwords, Microsoft 365 SSO tokens and Wi-Fi credentials [S1]. FruitStone is a web C2 panel branded 'CloudSync Console' with multi-operator support, proxy relay management, SNI-spoofed beacon profiles and a payload campaign builder [S1]. Stolen tokens are used for cloud access, and doppelganger domains support adversary-in-the-middle and device code phishing against legitimate Microsoft sign-in pages [S1]. Microsoft says AI supports a significant portion of operations and that ChocoShell code comments may indicate AI-assisted generation [S1].

campaigns.name: AI-augmented device code and OAuth phishing
campaigns.summary: Storm-2945 begins device code and OAuth phishing leading to Entra device registration and Microsoft 365 data collection [S1].

campaigns.name: CaptiveCrunch captive-portal traffic manipulation begins
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observes traffic manipulation through captive portal networks from early May; widespread compromise of Wi-Fi networks at hospitality-related organizations in several countries [S1]. ms365-live[.]com first seen 2026-05-14 [S1].

campaigns.name: Malware and AitM infrastructure build-out
campaigns.summary: CornFlake and ChocoShell hashes first seen 3 and 10 July; device code redirects on some landing pages from 16 July; ReliaQuest reports doppelganger domains used for AitM phishing on 23 July [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft publishes CaptiveCrunch report
campaigns.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence names Storm-2945 and CaptiveCrunch and releases detections, hunting queries and mitigations; acknowledges Anthropic, OpenAI and Google Threat Intelligence Group [S1].

campaigns.name: CaptiveCrunch resumes
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's 5 October update reports renewed activity from 29 September, reusing upstream hospitality managed service provider access; newer redirect domains and IPs first seen 30 September to 1 October; a Rust CornFlake variant observed [S1].

diamond.adversary: Storm-2945, assessed by Microsoft as an operational sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard [S1].
diamond.capability: CornFlake Go RAT, ChocoShell PowerShell infostealer, FruitStone C2 panel, ClickFix and fake-update lures, device code and AitM phishing, AI-assisted operations [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised captive portal and Wi-Fi equipment; redirect domains such as cdn-gstat[.]com, sslcdnhost[.]com and network-privacy[.]com; doppelganger domains such as ms365-live[.]com, ms365-device[.]com, m365-owa[.]com and owa-ms365[.]com; ChocoShell C2 213.145.86[.]112 [S1].
diamond.victim: Corporate travelers on hospitality and conference guest Wi-Fi, and hospitality organizations and possibly their managed service providers as access vectors [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Microsoft links the sub-cluster to Midnight Blizzard, whose typical targets are governments, diplomatic entities, NGOs and IT service providers mainly in the US and Europe [S1]. Direct state tasking for CaptiveCrunch is not stated in Microsoft's post [S1].
diamond.technology: Captive portal appliances and shared management systems, connectivity-check behavior (DNS/HTTP), Microsoft 365 and Entra device code flow, browser credential stores, Windows user-level persistence [S1].

gaps: Initial compromise vector for the captive portal networks is still under investigation per Microsoft [S1].
Microsoft's post lists no specific countries or victim organizations [S1].

Secondary press attributes specific details (exposed SSH/SNMP/web admin interfaces with weak credentials; gateways in several US cities, India and Saudi Arabia; victim traffic from finance, healthcare, legal, energy, retail and professional services; Black Lotus Labs finding of about 70 IPs across three North American providers at moderate confidence) to ReliaQuest and Black Lotus Labs. The original reports were not opened and these details are unverified here.
Original ReliaQuest and Black Lotus Labs publications and the Zscaler write-up were not retrieved.
Some press headlines label the campaign APT28-linked; this conflicts with Microsoft's Midnight Blizzard assessment and is unresolved in the sources gathered [S1].
No government (SVR) attribution specific to Storm-2945 or CaptiveCrunch was found.
Boundary between Storm-2945 and the wider Midnight Blizzard cluster and Storm-2372 is Microsoft's overlap assessment only; no MITRE group ID exists for Storm-2945.
The Microsoft fetch returned a summarized page; exact wording and full IOC list should be checked against the original post.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain includes hotel and conference guest Wi-Fi, captive portal appliances and their hospitality managed service providers, and traveler endpoints carrying cloud SSO tokens [S1]. STEP 2: Travelers are exposed whenever they use venue networks and rely on browser connectivity checks, and device code flow plus unmanaged Wi-Fi widen the window [S1]. STEP 3: The observed pattern is portal compromise, DNS/HTTP redirection, ClickFix or fake update lure, CornFlake/ChocoShell, token theft, then cloud access, with AitM and device code phishing as follow-on [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic and targeted credential and session theft from travelers on hospitality networks, redeployed quickly through retained provider access, as seen on 29 September 2026 [S1]. MDCOA is use of the same access against traveling government, defense or contractor personnel at conferences and TDYs to reach cloud-hosted mission data, with AI shortening development cycles [S1]. Candidate indicators: connectivity-check traffic followed by unexpected downloads, Windows service 'Cloud Sync Service', %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe, AMSI tampering or UAC bypass alerts, device code sign-ins from unexpected locations, and the listed domains and IPs [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Microsoft's CaptiveCrunch updates and IOC refreshes (initial 31 July, updated 5 October 2026) and correlate with personnel travel and conference schedules [S1]. (2) Authorities: blocking device code flow, Conditional Access and managed-device Wi-Fi restrictions are enterprise policy actions that need the appropriate network owner approvals [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: treat guest and venue networks as untrusted, prefer hotspots, eSIM or enterprise travel routers with VPN, and use phishing-resistant MFA to protect cloud-hosted mission data [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with the cloud and identity providers and relevant defense cyber partners; note that Microsoft warns some Russia-linked alerts may stem from other actors, so avoid attributing without corroboration [S1].
